partner_context.their_ambition: Sydney already runs one of the world's iconic public ferry networks - ten routes, ~38 wharves, Opal-integrated. Transport for NSW plans, contracts and regulates all public transport in New South Wales — trains, metro, light rail, buses and the Sydney Ferries network. Ferries are an integrated Opal-fare public mode across Sydney Harbour and the Parramatta River, operated under contract on the F1-F10 routes.
partner_context.their_pressure: NSW has committed to a zero-emission transport fleet; the first NSW electric ferry is planned for the new Sydney Fish Market route from 2029. Growth and the net-zero mandate both demand fleet renewal without disturbing the services people rely on today.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the software-defined, zero-emission foiling upgrade to a public ferry mode Sydney already runs at scale. Foiling hulls are faster, near-silent and low-wake - ideal for the wake-sensitive Parramatta River and for fast cross-harbour hops - while the heritage Manly and inner-harbour services continue underneath.

hero.title: A zero-emission ferry network for Sydney Harbour
hero.subtitle: A foiling tier above today's ferry network on Sydney Harbour and the Parramatta River: faster, near-silent, low-wake lines, a clear decarbonization path, and the services people rely on left running underneath.
hero.what_we_do_together: Navier is the software-defined, zero-emission foiling upgrade to a public ferry mode Sydney already runs at scale. Foiling hulls are faster, near-silent and low-wake - ideal for the wake-sensitive Parramatta River and for fast cross-harbour hops - while the heritage Manly and inner-harbour services continue underneath.

why_now: A zero-emission foiling tier is exactly the fleet renewal the net-zero mandate requires - faster and quieter than the current RiverCat/Emerald displacement fleet, and able to open low-wake river and cross-harbour lines. NSW has committed to a zero-emission transport fleet; the first NSW electric ferry is planned for the new Sydney Fish Market route from 2029. A demo vessel is on the water now.
multimodal_fit: Navier slots into the network as the fast marine mode on Sydney Harbour and the Parramatta River — feeding the existing rail, metro and bus interchanges and adding lines toward the authority's published growth and net-zero targets.

objections.concern: Will this disturb the heritage Manly and inner-harbour services?
objections.response: No — the foiling tier runs above the existing network on faster, low-wake lines. The iconic Manly and inner-harbour services continue underneath; this is purely additive fleet renewal.
Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal at existing piers — no new shore power, vertiports or rights-of-way.

objections.concern: Is foiling safe in busy, shared public waterways?
objections.response: Foiling is software-governed — geofenced no-foil and low-wake zones near piers, ferry lanes and moorings, automatic speed and wake limits in shared water, and conventional low-speed handling everywhere it isn't cleared to fly.

close.title: A zero-emission water layer that grows with the city.
close.body: Start on the busiest commuter corridors, scale across the full Sydney Harbour and the Parramatta River network, then mature the service — a zero-emission foiling tier that advances the authority's net-zero mandate while the services people rely on keep running underneath.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop — roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time. A step-change in marine mobility, not an incremental faster boat.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists — the open water and the piers already in use. No vertiports, no new rights-of-way, no tunnels or tracks. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the long-range hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all. Nothing to permit, build, or wait for.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Three forces just converged: the technology crossed from prototype to platform (10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out), decarbonization mandates turned legacy diesel fleets into stranded liabilities, and the hybrid removed the charging excuse. Autonomy is arriving on the water before the road. The marine layer is being claimed cluster-by-cluster right now.
